levels.title: What is HTML
levels.description:
HTML stands for **HyperText Markup Language**. It is the standard language used to create web pages. HTML uses **tags** to define elements on a page. 
Tags are written inside angle brackets like <tagname>.
levels.example:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My First Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    Hello World!
  </body>
</html>

levels.title: Paragraphs
levels.description:
Paragraphs are blocks of text. Use `

` tag to write them.
levels.example:
Hello, this is my first paragraph.

I love learning HTML!

levels.title: Links
levels.description: Links let you go from one page to another. Use the `<a>` tag with `href` (the web address).
levels.example: Go to Google

levels.title: Images
levels.description: Images make websites look nice. Use `` tag with `src` for the file and `alt` for text if the image doesn’t load.

levels.title: Lists
levels.description:
Lists help organize items. There are two types:

- **Ordered list `<ol>`** → numbered
- **Unordered list `<ul>`** → bullet points
levels.example:
1. First
  2. Second
  • Apples
  • Bananas

levels.title: Tables
levels.description: Tables help to show information in rows and columns. Use `<table>`, `<tr>` (row), `<td>` (cell).
levels.example:
NameAge
Alice10
Bob12

levels.title: Forms
levels.description: Forms are used to take input from users (like a login form). Use `<form>` with `<input>` and `<button>`.
levels.example:
Name:
Password:

levels.title: Audio
levels.description: The `<audio>` tag is used to play sound. You can add `controls` so the user can play/pause.
levels.example:
<audio controls>
  <source src='sound.mp3' type='audio/mpeg'>
  Your browser does not support the audio tag.
</audio>

levels.title: Video
levels.description: The `<video>` tag is used to play videos. You can add `controls` for play/pause.
levels.example:
<video width='320' height='240' controls>
  <source src='movie.mp4' type='video/mp4'>
  Your browser does not support the video tag.
</video>

levels.title: Semantic Tags
levels.description:
Semantic tags describe meaning. Examples:

- `<header>` → top of page
- `<nav>` → menu
- `<main>` → main content
- `<footer>` → bottom of page

They make code easier to read.
levels.example:
<header>Welcome to My Site</header>
<nav>Menu here</nav>
<main>Main content</main>
<footer>Copyright 2025</footer>

levels.title: Iframes
levels.description: An `<iframe>` shows another webpage inside your page. Like a window inside a window.
levels.example: <iframe src='https://www.wikipedia.org' width='400' height='300'></iframe>

levels.title: Meta Tags
levels.description: Meta tags give **information about the page**. They go inside `<head>`. For example, `charset` tells the text type and `viewport` makes the site mobile friendly.
levels.example:
<head>
  <meta charset='UTF-8'>
  <meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'>
</head>

levels.title: Forms Advanced
levels.description:
Forms can have many input types:

- `text`
- `email`
- `number`
- `checkbox`
- `radio`
- `date`

These help collect different data.
levels.example:
Email:
Age:
I agree
Male Female

levels.title: Forms + Labels
levels.description: Labels connect text with inputs, making forms easier to use.
levels.example:
<form>
  <label for='name'>Name:</label>
  <input type='text' id='name'>
</form>

levels.title: Div and Span
levels.description: `<div>` is a box for grouping elements. `<span>` is used for styling small parts of text.
levels.example:
This is inside a div.

This is red text.

levels.title: Comments
levels.description: Comments are notes for developers. They don’t show on the page. Use `<!-- -->`.
levels.example: Hello World

levels.title: Entities
levels.description:
Some symbols don’t work in HTML. Use **entities** instead:

- `<` → <
- `>` → >
- `&` → &
- `©` → ©
levels.example:
2 < 5

Copyright © 2025

levels.title: HTML5 Features
levels.description:
HTML5 brought new features:

- `<canvas>` → draw shapes
- `<video>` and `<audio>` → play media
- `<localStorage>` → store data in browser
levels.example: <canvas id='myCanvas' width='200' height='100' style='border:1px solid black;'></canvas>

levels.title: Best Practices
levels.description:
Some rules to follow:

- Always close tags
- Use lowercase for tags
- Keep code neat and clean
- Use semantic tags
- Add `alt` text for images
levels.example:
My Website

This is clean and simple code.

levels.title: HTML Attributes
levels.description:
Attributes provide **extra information** about elements. Example attributes include:

- `id` → unique identifier
- `class` → group for styling
- `style` → inline CSS
- `title` → tooltip text
levels.example: Hover over me to see tooltip.

levels.title: Block vs Inline Elements
levels.description:
HTML elements are either: - **Block-level** → start on a new line (e.g., `
`, `

`, `

`) - **Inline-level** → stay in line (e.g., ``, ``, ``)
levels.example: This is a blue word inside a paragraph.

levels.title: Inline vs External CSS
levels.description:
There are 3 ways to style HTML:

1. **Inline CSS** → style directly in the tag.
2. **Internal CSS** → inside `<style>` tag in `<head>`.
3. **External CSS** → linked `.css` file using `<link>` tag.
levels.example:
<head>
  <link rel='stylesheet' href='styles.css'>
</head>

levels.title: HTML Forms Validation
levels.description:
You can validate form inputs using HTML alone:

- `required` → must be filled
- `pattern` → regex check
- `min` / `max` → number limits
- `maxlength` → character limit
levels.example:
Email:
Age:

levels.title: HTML5 Input Types
levels.description:
HTML5 introduced new input types for better user experience:

- `color`
- `range`
- `file`
- `search`
- `url`
- `tel`
levels.example:
Favorite Color:
Search:
Website:

levels.title: Media Embedding
levels.description: You can embed content from other platforms like YouTube or Google Maps using `<iframe>`.
levels.example: <iframe width='560' height='315' src='https://www.youtube.com/embed/dQw4w9WgXcQ' allowfullscreen></iframe>

levels.title: HTML5 Data Attributes
levels.description: Custom `data-*` attributes store extra information on elements. These can be accessed via JavaScript.
levels.example: <button data-user='Sagar' data-level='Pro'>Click Me</button>

levels.title: HTML5 Local Storage
levels.description: `localStorage` lets you **store data in the browser** that stays even after refreshing or closing the page.
levels.example:
<script>
  localStorage.setItem('username', 'Sagar');
  console.log(localStorage.getItem('username')); // Output: Sagar
</script>

levels.title: HTML5 Session Storage
levels.description: `sessionStorage` is similar to localStorage but data **goes away when the browser is closed**.
levels.example:
<script>
  sessionStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
  console.log(sessionStorage.getItem('theme')); // Output: dark
</script>

levels.title: HTML Accessibility Basics
levels.description:
Accessibility helps people with disabilities use websites. Common practices:

- Use `alt` for images
- Add `aria-label` for screen readers
- Use proper heading hierarchy `<h1> - <h6>`
levels.example: <button aria-label='Play video'>▶</button>

levels.title: HTML5 Canvas Advanced
levels.description: The `<canvas>` element lets you **draw graphics and animations** using JavaScript.
levels.example:
<canvas id='myCanvas' width='200' height='100'></canvas>
<script>
  const canvas = document.getElementById('myCanvas');
  const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
  ctx.fillStyle = 'blue';
  ctx.fillRect(10, 10, 150, 80);
</script>

levels.title: HTML5 Geolocation API
levels.description: Geolocation API lets you **get the user's location** if they allow permission.
levels.example:
<script>
  navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(function(position) {
    console.log('Latitude:', position.coords.latitude);
    console.log('Longitude:', position.coords.longitude);
  });
</script>

levels.title: HTML5 Drag and Drop
levels.description: HTML5 supports drag-and-drop features for interactive UIs.
levels.example: Drag Me

levels.title: HTML5 Audio API
levels.description: Control audio programmatically with JavaScript using the HTML5 Audio API.
levels.example:
<audio id='myAudio' src='song.mp3'></audio>
<script>
  document.getElementById('myAudio').play();
</script>

levels.title: HTML5 Video with Captions
levels.description: You can add captions to videos using `<track>` tag.
levels.example:
<video controls>
  <source src='movie.mp4' type='video/mp4'>
  <track src='captions.vtt' kind='subtitles' srclang='en' label='English'>
</video>

levels.title: HTML SEO Basics
levels.description:
SEO (Search Engine Optimization) helps your website rank higher on Google. Best practices include:

- Use `<meta name='description'>`
- Proper heading structure
- Alt text for images
- Semantic tags
levels.example:
<head>
  <meta name='description' content='Learn HTML basics and advanced concepts.'>
</head>

levels.title: Responsive Web Design
levels.description: Use the `<meta viewport>` and CSS techniques like **flexbox** and **media queries** to make websites mobile-friendly.
levels.example:
<meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'>
<style>
  @media (max-width: 600px) {
    body { background: lightblue; }
  }
</style>

levels.title: HTML Best Practices (Advanced)
levels.description:
Follow these advanced rules for better HTML:

- Use `aria-` attributes for accessibility
- Keep structure semantic and minimal
- Validate your HTML using W3C Validator
- Optimize media with modern formats like WebP

levels.title: Progressive Web App (PWA) Basics
levels.description: HTML combined with JavaScript and service workers can create **PWA apps** that work offline and feel like native apps.
levels.example: <link rel='manifest' href='/manifest.json'>

levels.title: Final HTML Project
levels.description:
Build a full-featured HTML project with:

- Navigation bar
- Form with validation
- Video and audio player
- Responsive layout
- LocalStorage support
levels.example: My Site

levels.title: Selectors
levels.description: CSS selectors target HTML elements you want to style. Common selectors are element (like p), class (.class), and id (#id).

levels.title: Universal Selector
levels.description: The universal selector * selects every element on the page for styling.
levels.example: * { font-family: Arial; color: blue; }

levels.title: Grouping Selectors
levels.description: Group multiple selectors to apply the same style to them, separated by commas.
levels.example: h1, h2, p { text-align: center; color: purple; }

levels.title: Colors
levels.description: CSS lets you set background and text colors using names, hex codes, or rgb values.

levels.title: Fonts
levels.description: Change the font family, size, and style to make text look the way you want.
levels.example: p { font-family: 'Verdana'; font-size: 16px; font-style: italic; }

levels.title: Box Model
levels.description: Every element is a box with margin (space outside), border, and padding (space inside).
levels.example: div { margin: 10px; padding: 15px; border: 1px solid #888; }

levels.title: Width and Height
levels.description: Set how big elements appear using width and height in px, %, etc.
levels.example: img { width: 120px; height: 80px; }

levels.title: Backgrounds
levels.description: Add colors, gradients, or images as the background of elements.
levels.example:
body { background-image: url('photo.jpg'); }
.box { background: linear-gradient(orange, yellow); }

levels.title: Text Alignment & Spacing
levels.description: Align text and control its spacing: left, right, center; line height; letter spacing.
levels.example:
h2 { text-align: center; }
p { line-height: 1.8; letter-spacing: 1px; }

levels.title: Display & Position
levels.description: Choose how elements behave and where they’re placed: block, inline, fixed, absolute.
levels.example: .menu { display: block; position: fixed; top: 0; right: 0; }

levels.title: Flexbox
levels.description: Flexbox is a modern way to arrange items in rows or columns that adjust automatically.
levels.example: .container { display: flex; flex-direction: row; justify-content: space-between; }

levels.title: Responsive Design
levels.description: Media queries make designs adapt to different screen sizes, for phones and desktops.
levels.example: @media (max-width: 600px) { h1 { font-size: 18px; } .sidebar { display: none; } }

levels.title: Hover Effects
levels.description: Change the style of elements when the mouse is over them using :hover selectors.
levels.example:
a:hover { color: orange; }
button:hover { background: lightblue; }

levels.title: Transitions
levels.description: Make style changes smooth using transition, like animated background color on hover.
levels.example:
button { transition: background 0.3s; }
button:hover { background: teal; }

levels.title: Shadows
levels.description: Add drop shadows to boxes or text for a layered, modern look.
levels.example:
.card { box-shadow: 2px 2px 8px #ccc; }
h1 { text-shadow: 1px 1px 3px gray; }

levels.title: Border Radius
levels.description: Make corners rounded for boxes, buttons, images, etc.
levels.example:
img { border-radius: 50%; }
.button { border-radius: 8px; }

levels.title: Lists Styling
levels.description: Style bullet points, numbers, and spacing of lists for a custom look.
levels.example:
ul { list-style-type: circle; padding-left: 20px; }
ol { list-style-type: upper-alpha; }

levels.title: Z-index
levels.description: Use z-index to stack elements on top of or below each other when they overlap.
levels.example: .modal { position: absolute; z-index: 10; }

levels.title: Opacity
levels.description: Control how transparent an element is with opacity.
levels.example: .overlay { opacity: 0.5; }

levels.title: Comments
levels.description: Add comments in CSS using /* ... */ to explain your code. Browsers ignore comments.
levels.example:
/* This is a comment in CSS */
body { color: black; }

levels.title: Importing CSS
levels.description: Reuse code by importing CSS from another file using @import.
levels.example: @import url('theme.css');

levels.title: Gradients
levels.description: Create beautiful backgrounds with multiple colors using CSS gradients.
levels.example: body { background: linear-gradient(to right, #3498db, #e74c3c); }

levels.title: Text Truncation
levels.description: Truncate (cut off) long text and add ... using text-overflow.
levels.example: .truncate { width: 150px; white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }

levels.title: Introduction to JavaScript
levels.description: JavaScript is a powerful programming language used mainly to add interactivity to websites. It runs directly in the browser allowing dynamic content such as responding to clicks, validating forms, or updating page content without reloading. Beyond web browsers, JavaScript also powers servers, mobile apps, and more, making it a versatile language.
levels.example: console.log("Hello, World!");

levels.title: Variables and Data Types
levels.description: Variables in JavaScript are containers to store data values. You can declare variables using 'let', 'const', or 'var' (modern practice favors 'let' and 'const'). JavaScript supports various data types: Number for all numeric values, String for text, Boolean for true/false, null for intentional empty value, undefined for unassigned variables, Object for complex data, and Array for ordered lists.

levels.title: Operators
levels.description: Operators perform operations on variables and values. Arithmetic operators help perform calculations (+, -, *, /, %). Assignment operators assign values (=, +=, -=). Comparison operators (==, ===, !=, !==, >, <) are used to compare values. Logical operators (&&, ||, !) combine multiple conditions or negate them.
levels.example:
let x = 5 + 3;  // 8
let isEqual = (x === 8); // true
let isValid = (x > 5 && x < 10); // true

levels.title: Functions
levels.description: Functions are reusable blocks of code designed to perform a specific task. They can accept parameters as inputs and return outputs. Functions help organize code, reduce repetition, and improve readability. Functions can be declared traditionally, as function expressions, or using arrow function syntax introduced in ES6.

levels.title: Conditional Statements
levels.description: Conditional statements let your code make decisions by running different code blocks based on true or false conditions. The 'if', 'else if', and 'else' blocks allow multiple pathways. The switch statement provides an efficient way to select among many exact matches.

levels.title: Loops
levels.description: Loops allow you to repeat code multiple times, saving effort and code space. The 'for' loop runs a set number of times, 'while' repeats while a condition is true, and 'do...while' runs at least once before checking the condition. Loops are essential for iterating over arrays and handling repetitive tasks.

levels.title: Arrays
levels.description: Arrays store ordered collections of data. Each element has a numeric index starting at zero. Arrays can hold any data type, including other arrays or objects. Common array methods include push (add to end), pop (remove last), shift, unshift, map, filter, and reduce, to manipulate and transform data.

levels.title: Objects
levels.description: Objects are collections of key-value pairs that model real-world entities. Keys (properties) are strings, and values can be any type, including functions (called methods). Objects enable encapsulating data and behavior, a core part of JavaScript's flexibility.

levels.title: DOM Manipulation
levels.description: The Document Object Model (DOM) is a programming interface for HTML documents. JavaScript can select, modify, add, or delete HTML elements dynamically by manipulating the DOM. This capability powers interactive interfaces like content updates without page reloads, animations, and event handling.
levels.example:
const heading = document.querySelector('h1');
heading.textContent = 'Hello from JavaScript!';

levels.title: Events
levels.description: Events represent user interactions or browser actions like clicks, typing, or loading a page. JavaScript responds to events by attaching event listeners to elements, running functions when events occur. This interactivity makes websites dynamic and user-friendly.

levels.title: Advanced Functions
levels.description: Advanced function techniques include closures (functions retaining access to their lexical scope), higher-order functions (functions that take or return other functions), recursion (functions calling themselves), and arrow functions (concise syntax and different 'this' binding). These empower cleaner, modular code.

levels.title: Asynchronous JavaScript
levels.description: JavaScript runs in a single thread but handles asynchronous tasks like data fetching or timers using callbacks, promises, and async/await. These patterns prevent blocking the program while waiting for operations to complete, ensuring smooth user experiences.

levels.title: Error Handling
levels.description: JavaScript provides try-catch blocks to handle errors gracefully without stopping the entire program. Developers catch exceptions, log errors, and provide fallback behavior, improving program stability and user experience.

levels.title: ES6+ Features
levels.description: Modern JavaScript (ES6 and later) introduces enhancements like template literals (for easier string formatting), destructuring (extract values from arrays/objects), spread/rest operators, classes for object-oriented programming, modules for code organization, and many others making code concise and robust.

levels.title: Modules
levels.description: Modules let you split your code into separate files and reuse code by exporting and importing variables, functions, or classes. This helps keep large applications organized and maintainable.

levels.title: Object-Oriented Programming
levels.description: JavaScript supports OOP using prototypes and ES6 classes. Classes enable defining blueprints for objects, including properties and methods. Key concepts include inheritance, encapsulation, and polymorphism, allowing complex and reusable code structures.

levels.title: Promises and Async/Await
levels.description: Promises represent future values in asynchronous code, helping manage sequences of async tasks. Async/await syntax makes asynchronous code look synchronous, simplifying complex chains and improving readability.

levels.title: JavaScript Design Patterns
levels.description: Design patterns provide reusable solutions to common coding problems. Familiar patterns in JavaScript include Module, Singleton, Factory, Observer, and Prototype. Understanding these helps create modular, maintainable, and scalable code.

levels.title: Memory Management and Optimization
levels.description: Effective JavaScript programming requires awareness of memory usage. Understanding garbage collection, avoiding memory leaks, and writing optimized code improves performance especially in large-scale or long-running apps.

levels.title: Testing and Debugging
levels.description: Testing ensures code works as expected; JavaScript has tools like Jest, Mocha, and Jasmine for unit testing. Debugging techniques include using browser developer tools, console logging, and step-by-step code tracing to locate and fix bugs.

levels.title: Introduction to React.js
levels.description: React.js is a popular JavaScript library for building user interfaces, especially single-page applications (SPAs). It uses a component-based architecture, where UI elements are created as reusable, independent pieces. React makes use of a virtual DOM for efficient rendering and updates, improving performance.

levels.title: JSX Syntax
levels.description: JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension for JavaScript used in React to describe what the UI should look like. It allows you to write HTML-like code directly within JavaScript. JSX makes code more readable and expressive. It is compiled into regular JavaScript under the hood.
levels.example:
const element =

Welcome to React!

; console.log(element);

levels.title: Components
levels.description: Components are the building blocks of a React application. They can be **functional** or **class-based**. Functional components are preferred in modern React due to their simplicity and support for hooks. Each component can accept inputs called props and return JSX.

levels.title: Props
levels.description: Props (short for properties) allow data to be passed from a parent component to a child component. They are **read-only** and help make components reusable and dynamic.

levels.title: State and useState Hook
levels.description: State allows components to keep track of dynamic data and re-render when that data changes. In functional components, the `useState` hook is used to manage state.

levels.title: useEffect Hook
levels.description: `useEffect` is used to perform side effects in functional components, such as fetching data, updating the DOM, or setting up timers. It runs after the component renders.

levels.title: Handling Events
levels.description: React uses event handlers similar to HTML, but with camelCase syntax. Events like clicks, form submissions, or key presses are handled using functions.

levels.title: Conditional Rendering
levels.description: Conditional rendering lets you display different UI elements depending on certain conditions, using `if` statements, the ternary operator, or logical operators.

levels.title: Lists and Keys
levels.description: You can render lists in React by using the `map()` function. Each item should have a unique key to help React identify which items have changed, been added, or removed.

levels.title: React Router Basics
levels.description: React Router is used for adding navigation to your application. It allows you to create different routes and switch between components without reloading the page.

levels.title: Context API
levels.description: The Context API allows you to share data across multiple components without having to pass props down manually at every level. It's ideal for global data like themes, user authentication, or settings.

levels.title: Custom Hooks
levels.description: Custom hooks let you extract and reuse stateful logic across multiple components. They are regular functions whose names start with 'use'.

levels.title: Forms and Controlled Components
levels.description: Controlled components are form elements like inputs and textareas that are controlled by React state. Their values are updated via state and event handlers.

levels.title: Refs and useRef Hook
levels.description: Refs are used to directly access DOM elements or persist values across renders without causing re-renders. The `useRef` hook helps manage these references.

levels.title: useMemo and useCallback
levels.description: React provides `useMemo` and `useCallback` hooks to optimize performance by memoizing values and functions. This prevents unnecessary recalculations and re-renders.

levels.title: Error Boundaries
levels.description: Error boundaries catch JavaScript errors in child components and display a fallback UI instead of crashing the entire app. They must be class components.

levels.title: React Lazy Loading and Suspense
levels.description: Lazy loading lets you load components only when they are needed, improving performance. `Suspense` allows you to show a fallback UI while components are loading.

levels.title: Performance Optimization with React.memo
levels.description: `React.memo` prevents a component from re-rendering unless its props have changed. This is useful for components that receive the same props frequently.

levels.title: React Portals
levels.description: Portals allow you to render children into a DOM node outside of the parent component hierarchy. This is useful for modals, tooltips, and pop-ups.

levels.title: React Testing with Jest and React Testing Library
levels.description: Testing ensures your components work correctly. Jest is a testing framework, and React Testing Library provides utilities to test React components effectively.

levels.title: React with TypeScript
levels.description: TypeScript adds static type checking to React, making your code more robust and easier to maintain. You define types for props, state, and hooks.

levels.title: Code Splitting
levels.description: Code splitting breaks your application into smaller bundles that can be loaded on demand. This improves initial load times.

levels.title: Deployment
levels.description: You can deploy React apps to various platforms like Vercel, Netlify, or GitHub Pages. Use `npm run build` to create an optimized production build.
levels.example:
npm run build
# After build, deploy the 'build' folder to your hosting platform.

levels.title: React and APIs
levels.description: React works seamlessly with APIs to fetch and display data. You can use the Fetch API or libraries like Axios to handle HTTP requests.

levels.title: Server-Side Rendering (SSR) with Next.js
levels.description: Next.js enables server-side rendering and static site generation for React apps, improving performance and SEO.

levels.title: Introduction to Next.js
levels.description: Next.js is a React framework for building fast, production-grade web applications. It provides features like server-side rendering (SSR), static site generation (SSG), API routes, and optimized performance out of the box.
levels.example:
npx create-next-app@latest my-next-app
cd my-next-app
npm run dev

levels.title: File-based Routing
levels.description: Next.js uses a file-based routing system. Any file you create in the 'pages' folder automatically becomes a route in your application.

levels.title: Linking Between Pages
levels.description: Use the `Link` component from Next.js to navigate between pages without reloading the browser, providing a seamless single-page app experience.

levels.title: Dynamic Routes
levels.description: You can create dynamic routes by using square brackets in the filename. This is useful for pages like blog posts, product pages, or user profiles.

levels.title: Static Site Generation (SSG)
levels.description: SSG generates HTML at build time. Use `getStaticProps` to fetch data before rendering the page. Ideal for pages with content that doesn’t change frequently.

levels.title: Static Paths with Dynamic Routes
levels.description: When using dynamic routes with SSG, you must define paths to pre-render using `getStaticPaths`.

levels.title: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
levels.description: Use `getServerSideProps` to fetch data on every request. This is useful for dynamic content that changes frequently, like dashboards or live data.

levels.title: API Routes
levels.description: Next.js allows you to create serverless API endpoints inside the `pages/api` folder. Each file in this folder becomes an endpoint.

levels.title: Environment Variables
levels.description: Store sensitive data like API keys using environment variables. Use `.env.local` for development and `process.env` to access them in code.

levels.title: Image Optimization
levels.description: Next.js has a built-in Image component that optimizes images automatically. It supports lazy loading and resizing on the fly.

levels.title: API Fetching with SWR
levels.description: SWR is a React hook library for data fetching. It handles caching, revalidation, focus tracking, and more automatically.

levels.title: Middleware
levels.description: Middleware lets you run code before a request is completed, useful for authentication, logging, or redirects. Create a `_middleware.js` file inside your pages folder.

levels.title: Custom App and Document
levels.description: Customize the default App and Document to modify how pages are rendered. `_app.js` wraps all pages, and `_document.js` customizes the HTML document structure.

levels.title: API Authentication
levels.description: You can handle authentication using JSON Web Tokens (JWT) or OAuth inside Next.js API routes. Protect pages and endpoints based on user sessions.

levels.title: API Caching and Revalidation
levels.description: Next.js supports Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) to revalidate pages after they’ve been built. This enables static pages to stay up-to-date.

levels.title: Internationalization (i18n)
levels.description: Next.js has built-in support for internationalization (i18n), making it easy to create multilingual websites.

levels.title: API Error Handling
levels.description: Handle errors gracefully in API routes by returning appropriate HTTP status codes and JSON error messages.

levels.title: Deploying a Next.js App
levels.description: Next.js apps can be deployed to Vercel (official platform), Netlify, or other cloud services. Vercel offers seamless integration with GitHub and GitLab.
levels.example:
npm run build
npm run start
# Deploy by pushing to a Git repository connected to Vercel.

levels.title: Optimizing Performance
levels.description: Use built-in tools like automatic code splitting, lazy loading, image optimization, and caching headers to make your Next.js app faster.

levels.title: Full Stack Next.js Example
levels.description: Combine all concepts to create a full-stack app: static pages, server-side rendering, API routes, authentication, and deployment.

levels.title: Introduction to Node.js
levels.description: Node.js is a runtime environment that allows you to run JavaScript code on the server side. It uses the V8 JavaScript engine and is designed for building scalable, high-performance applications. Node.js is event-driven and non-blocking, making it ideal for real-time applications like chat apps, streaming services, and APIs.
levels.example: console.log('Hello from Node.js!');

levels.title: Installing Node.js and npm
levels.description: To get started with Node.js, install it from the official website. Node.js comes with npm (Node Package Manager) pre-installed, which allows you to install and manage packages and libraries. Verify installation by running `node -v` and `npm -v` in your terminal.
levels.example:
node -v
npm -v

levels.title: Creating Your First Node.js App
levels.description: You can create a simple Node.js app by using the built-in 'http' module to set up a basic server. This server listens for requests and responds with a message, demonstrating the core of Node.js functionality.

levels.title: Modules and require()
levels.description: Node.js uses modules to organize code. You can use built-in modules like 'fs', 'path', and 'http', or create your own custom modules. The `require()` function is used to import modules into your application.

levels.title: File System Module (fs)
levels.description: The 'fs' module allows you to interact with the file system. You can read, write, update, and delete files using this module, making it essential for backend development in Node.js.

levels.title: npm and Packages
levels.description: npm is used to manage external libraries and packages in Node.js. You can initialize a project with `npm init` and install packages using `npm install`. Popular packages include Express, Mongoose, and Lodash.
levels.example:
npm init -y
npm install express

levels.title: Building a Simple API with Express
levels.description: Express is a lightweight framework for building web servers and APIs in Node.js. It simplifies handling routes, middleware, and requests/responses.

levels.title: Middleware in Express
levels.description: Middleware functions are used in Express to process requests before sending responses. They can be used for tasks like authentication, logging, or parsing request bodies.

levels.title: Environment Variables
levels.description: Environment variables store configuration data outside of your code, such as database URLs or API keys. Use the 'dotenv' package to load variables from a `.env` file into your application.

levels.title: Connecting to MongoDB
levels.description: MongoDB is a popular NoSQL database often used with Node.js. You can connect to it using the Mongoose library, which provides a schema-based solution to model your data.

levels.title: Building a REST API
levels.description: A REST API allows communication between a server and client using HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE. You can combine Express and Mongoose to create CRUD endpoints for a database.

levels.title: Error Handling
levels.description: Error handling is crucial for building robust applications. Use try-catch blocks, middleware, and proper response codes to handle errors gracefully.

levels.title: Authentication with JWT
levels.description: JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are commonly used for user authentication. The server issues a token after login, which the client sends with each request for verification.

levels.title: EventEmitter
levels.description: Node.js uses an event-driven architecture. The EventEmitter class lets you create and handle custom events in your application.

levels.title: Streams in Node.js
levels.description: Streams handle data in chunks, making them efficient for reading and writing large files. There are four types: Readable, Writable, Duplex, and Transform streams.

levels.title: Deploying Node.js Apps
levels.description: You can deploy Node.js apps to hosting platforms like Heroku, Vercel, or AWS. Make sure to set up environment variables, production scripts, and security practices before deployment.
levels.example:
// Example deployment command
heroku create
heroku config:set NODE_ENV=production
heroku push origin main

levels.title: Clustering in Node.js
levels.description: Node.js runs on a single thread by default, which can limit performance on multi-core systems. The 'cluster' module allows you to spawn multiple worker processes that share the same server port, improving scalability and performance.

levels.title: WebSockets with Socket.IO
levels.description: WebSockets enable real-time, bi-directional communication between clients and the server. The 'socket.io' package is a popular library for implementing WebSockets in Node.js applications, ideal for chat apps or live notifications.

levels.title: Caching with Redis
levels.description: Caching improves performance by storing frequently accessed data in memory. Redis is a popular in-memory data store that integrates seamlessly with Node.js, reducing database calls and speeding up responses.

levels.title: Rate Limiting
levels.description: Rate limiting prevents abuse of APIs by restricting the number of requests a client can make within a certain timeframe. It's essential for protecting your server from overload or malicious attacks.

levels.title: Logging with Winston
levels.description: Logging is vital for debugging and monitoring production apps. The Winston library provides a flexible logging system with multiple transport options like console, files, or external services.

levels.title: Asynchronous Programming with Promises and Async/Await
levels.description: Node.js is asynchronous by default. Understanding Promises and async/await is essential for writing clean, non-blocking code while handling asynchronous operations like database queries or API requests.

levels.title: Worker Threads
levels.description: The 'worker_threads' module allows you to run JavaScript code in parallel threads. This is useful for CPU-intensive tasks like image processing or data encryption, which would otherwise block the main thread.

levels.title: Microservices Architecture
levels.description: Microservices involve breaking a large application into smaller, independent services that communicate via APIs or messaging queues. This architecture makes scaling and maintenance easier.

levels.title: Message Queues with RabbitMQ
levels.description: Message queues help microservices communicate reliably and asynchronously. RabbitMQ is a popular message broker for decoupling services and improving fault tolerance.

levels.title: GraphQL API with Node.js
levels.description: GraphQL is an alternative to REST APIs that allows clients to request only the data they need. You can use libraries like Apollo Server to build a GraphQL API in Node.js.

levels.title: Testing with Jest
levels.description: Testing is essential to ensure code quality and prevent bugs. Jest is a popular testing framework for Node.js that allows you to write unit and integration tests easily.

levels.title: Scaling Node.js with Docker
levels.description: Docker allows you to containerize your Node.js applications, making them portable and easier to deploy across different environments. Containers are lightweight and ideal for microservices.
levels.example:
// Dockerfile
FROM node:18
WORKDIR /usr/src/app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

levels.title: Security Best Practices
levels.description: Security is crucial for production applications. Best practices include validating inputs, using HTTPS, protecting against SQL injection and XSS, and securely storing secrets.

levels.title: Monitoring and Performance
levels.description: Monitoring tools help track app health, performance, and error rates. Tools like PM2, New Relic, and Datadog are commonly used to monitor production Node.js apps.

levels.title: Integrating AI with Node.js
levels.description: You can integrate AI into your Node.js apps by connecting with AI APIs such as OpenAI, Hugging Face, or TensorFlow.js. This allows you to add features like natural language processing, sentiment analysis, and image recognition.

levels.title: TensorFlow.js for Machine Learning
levels.description: TensorFlow.js lets you run machine learning models directly in Node.js. You can train models or load pre-trained ones for tasks like image classification, speech recognition, or predictive analytics.

levels.title: Blockchain Basics with Node.js
levels.description: Blockchain technology can be used to create decentralized apps (dApps). Using Node.js, you can build blockchain networks or interact with popular blockchains like Ethereum through Web3.js.

levels.title: Smart Contracts with Ethereum
levels.description: Node.js can be used to deploy and interact with smart contracts on Ethereum. Smart contracts are self-executing programs that run on the blockchain, commonly used in dApps and NFTs.

levels.title: Building a dApp Backend
levels.description: A decentralized application (dApp) often needs a traditional backend to store off-chain data, user authentication, and interactions with the blockchain network.

levels.title: Continuous Integration with GitHub Actions
levels.description: CI/CD pipelines automate the process of testing and deploying code. GitHub Actions can run automated tests and deploy your Node.js application whenever you push updates to your repository.
levels.example:
// .github/workflows/nodejs.yml
name: Node.js CI

on: [push]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v2
      - name: Setup Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v2
        with:
          node-version: '18'
      - run: npm install
      - run: npm test

levels.title: Advanced Docker with Kubernetes
levels.description: Kubernetes is a container orchestration system that automates scaling, deployment, and management of Node.js containers. It is ideal for microservices and cloud-native applications.
levels.example:
// deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-app
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-app
        image: my-node-app:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000

levels.title: Serverless Functions with AWS Lambda
levels.description: Serverless architecture allows you to run functions on demand without managing servers. AWS Lambda is a popular platform for deploying Node.js functions triggered by events like HTTP requests or database updates.

levels.title: Advanced Authentication with OAuth 2.0
levels.description: OAuth 2.0 is a secure authentication standard widely used by platforms like Google and Facebook. It allows users to log into your application using third-party accounts without sharing their passwords.

levels.title: Real-Time Analytics Dashboard
levels.description: Create real-time analytics dashboards using Node.js, WebSockets, and a database like Redis or MongoDB. This is useful for monitoring user activity, financial data, or IoT devices.

levels.title: Distributed Systems with gRPC
levels.description: gRPC is a high-performance framework for connecting services in distributed systems. It uses protocol buffers for efficient data serialization and works well for microservices communication.

levels.title: CI/CD with Jenkins
levels.description: Jenkins is a popular tool for automating builds, tests, and deployments. It integrates well with Node.js projects and can be part of a robust CI/CD pipeline.

levels.title: Event-Driven Microservices
levels.description: Event-driven architecture uses events to trigger communication between microservices. This allows services to be loosely coupled and scalable, often implemented with message queues like Kafka or RabbitMQ.

levels.title: Scaling to Millions of Users
levels.description: Scaling Node.js applications to millions of users involves a combination of horizontal scaling, load balancing, caching, and microservices architecture. Tools like NGINX, Redis, and Kubernetes play crucial roles.

levels.title: Final Project: Full Stack Enterprise App
levels.description: Combine everything learned to build a production-ready full stack app with authentication, real-time features, microservices, CI/CD pipelines, Kubernetes deployment, and monitoring dashboards.

levels.title: Introduction to Express.js
levels.description: Express.js is a minimal and flexible Node.js web application framework that provides a robust set of features for building web and mobile applications. It simplifies handling HTTP requests, routing, and middleware.

levels.title: Installing Express.js
levels.description: To use Express, install it using npm. Then, require it in your project and create an app instance to start building your server.
levels.example:
npm init -y
npm install express

levels.title: Basic Routing
levels.description: Routing determines how an application responds to client requests at specific endpoints. Express provides methods like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE for handling different HTTP requests.

levels.title: Middleware Basics
levels.description: Middleware functions are functions that have access to the request and response objects. They are used for logging, authentication, parsing request bodies, and more.

levels.title: Serving Static Files
levels.description: Express makes it easy to serve static files like HTML, CSS, and images by using the built-in express.static middleware.
levels.example:
app.use(express.static('public'));
// Access files via http://localhost:3000/filename

levels.title: Express JSON Middleware
levels.description: To handle JSON data sent by clients, Express provides built-in middleware to parse JSON request bodies.

levels.title: Route Parameters and Query Strings
levels.description: Express allows you to capture values from URLs using route parameters and query strings for dynamic routing.

levels.title: Using Template Engines
levels.description: Template engines like EJS or Pug allow you to dynamically generate HTML pages from data on the server.

levels.title: Modular Routes
levels.description: Separate routes into different files for cleaner, more maintainable code by using express.Router().

levels.title: Error Handling Middleware
levels.description: Handle errors globally by creating a custom middleware that captures errors and returns a proper response to the client.

levels.title: Express with MongoDB
levels.description: Integrate Express with a database like MongoDB using Mongoose to store and retrieve data dynamically.

levels.title: Building a RESTful API
levels.description: Create a REST API with Express by handling different HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE for CRUD operations.

levels.title: Authentication with JWT
levels.description: Use JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for secure authentication in your Express app.

levels.title: CORS in Express
levels.description: Enable Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) so your API can be accessed from different domains securely.

levels.title: Express and File Uploads
levels.description: Handle file uploads using the Multer middleware in Express.

levels.title: Rate Limiting and Security
levels.description: Add security to your API by limiting requests and preventing common attacks like brute force or DDoS.

levels.title: Logging and Debugging
levels.description: Use tools like Morgan or Winston for logging requests and errors to help with debugging and monitoring.

levels.title: Testing Express Apps
levels.description: Test your Express app using tools like Mocha, Chai, or Jest to ensure it works as expected.

levels.title: WebSockets with Express
levels.description: Integrate WebSockets into your Express app to build real-time features like chat applications or live notifications.

levels.title: Deploying an Express App
levels.description: Deploy your Express app to platforms like Heroku, AWS, or Vercel by setting up production scripts and environment variables.

levels.title: Cluster Mode for Scaling
levels.description: Node.js runs on a single thread by default. Express apps can use the Node.js 'cluster' module to run multiple instances across CPU cores, improving performance and handling more concurrent requests.

levels.title: Load Balancing Express Apps
levels.description: Distribute traffic across multiple Express app instances using a reverse proxy or load balancer like Nginx or PM2 to improve reliability and uptime.

levels.title: Using PM2 for Process Management
levels.description: PM2 is a production process manager for Node.js applications that helps manage multiple instances, load balancing, logging, and auto-restarts.
levels.example:
npm install pm2 -g

# Start app with PM2
pm2 start index.js -i max

# Monitor app
pm2 logs
pm2 monit

levels.title: Microservices with Express
levels.description: Break large monolithic apps into smaller microservices, each handling a specific domain or functionality. This improves scalability and code maintainability.

levels.title: API Gateway Integration
levels.description: An API gateway acts as a single entry point for clients and routes requests to different microservices, handling authentication, rate-limiting, and logging.

levels.title: Message Queues with Express
levels.description: Use message brokers like RabbitMQ or Kafka to enable asynchronous communication between services, preventing bottlenecks in your Express app.

levels.title: Caching with Redis
levels.description: Improve performance by caching frequently requested data using Redis. This reduces database load and response time for repetitive queries.

levels.title: WebSockets for Real-Time Features
levels.description: Add real-time capabilities like live chat, notifications, or tracking using WebSockets with libraries like Socket.IO.

levels.title: GraphQL with Express
levels.description: Integrate GraphQL into your Express app to create flexible APIs with strongly typed schemas and resolvers.

levels.title: Dockerizing Express Apps
levels.description: Containerize your Express app using Docker to ensure consistent deployments across different environments.
levels.example:
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "index.js"]

levels.title: Server-Side Rendering (SSR)
levels.description: Use Express to serve pre-rendered HTML for SEO-friendly and faster-loading pages, often paired with frontend frameworks like React or Next.js.

levels.title: Monitoring and Performance Metrics
levels.description: Monitor your Express app's performance using tools like New Relic, Datadog, or Prometheus to identify bottlenecks and improve response times.

levels.title: Scaling Databases for Express
levels.description: Learn how to scale your database to handle high traffic using read replicas, sharding, and connection pooling techniques.

levels.title: Advanced Security Best Practices
levels.description: Secure your Express app by implementing Helmet, sanitizing inputs, and following OWASP guidelines to prevent attacks like XSS and CSRF.

levels.title: Final Deployment and Scaling Strategy

            - containerPort: 3000

levels.title: Algorithm
levels.description: An algorithm is a step-by-step set of instructions designed to solve a specific problem or perform a task. Algorithms form the foundation of computer programs.

levels.title: Variable
levels.description: A variable is a container used to store data in a program. It allows you to label and manipulate data values.

levels.title: Data Type
levels.description: Data types define the kind of data a variable can hold, such as numbers, strings, booleans, arrays, and objects.
levels.example:
let number = 42; // Number
let text = 'Hello'; // String
let isActive = true; // Boolean
let list = [1, 2, 3]; // Array

levels.title: Conditional Statement
levels.description: Conditional statements allow programs to make decisions based on conditions, typically using if, else if, and else.

levels.title: Loop
levels.description: Loops are used to repeat a block of code multiple times until a certain condition is met.

levels.title: Function
levels.description: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Functions help keep code modular and organized.

levels.title: Array
levels.description: An array is a data structure that can store multiple values in a single variable. The values can be accessed by their index number.
levels.example:
let fruits = ['Apple', 'Banana', 'Mango'];
console.log(fruits[1]); // Output: Banana

levels.title: Object
levels.description: An object stores data in key-value pairs and is used to represent complex data structures.

levels.title: Class
levels.description: A class is a blueprint for creating objects with shared properties and methods. It is a core concept in object-oriented programming (OOP).

levels.title: API
levels.description: An API (Application Programming Interface) defines how different software components should communicate with each other.

levels.title: Recursion
levels.description: Recursion is a technique where a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the problem until it reaches a base case.

levels.title: Asynchronous Programming
levels.description: Asynchronous programming allows a program to handle tasks like network requests without blocking the main thread, improving performance and responsiveness.

levels.title: Promise
levels.description: A Promise represents a value that may be available now, later, or never. It is commonly used for handling asynchronous operations in JavaScript.

levels.title: Big O Notation
levels.description: Big O notation describes the efficiency of an algorithm in terms of time complexity and space complexity as the input size grows.

levels.title: Hashing
levels.description: Hashing converts data into a fixed-size string, often used for storing passwords securely or indexing data efficiently.

levels.title: REST
levels.description: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style for designing networked APIs that use HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE.
levels.example:
GET /users
POST /users
PUT /users/:id
DELETE /users/:id

levels.title: GraphQL
levels.description: GraphQL is a query language for APIs that allows clients to request only the data they need, reducing over-fetching.

levels.title: Concurrency
levels.description: Concurrency is the ability of a system to execute multiple tasks at overlapping times without necessarily running them simultaneously.

levels.title: Multithreading
levels.description: Multithreading allows a program to run multiple threads in parallel, improving performance for CPU-intensive tasks.

levels.title: Containerization
levels.description: Containerization packages applications and their dependencies into isolated environments to ensure consistent deployments across systems. Docker is a popular containerization tool.
levels.example:
# Dockerfile Example
FROM node:18-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm install
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "index.js"]

levels.title: Stack
levels.description: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last In, First Out (LIFO) principle. It is commonly used in function calls, undo operations, and expression evaluation.

levels.title: Queue
levels.description: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First In, First Out (FIFO) principle. It is used in task scheduling and handling asynchronous data.

levels.title: Linked List
levels.description: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are connected using pointers, allowing dynamic memory allocation and efficient insertions/deletions.

levels.title: Tree
levels.description: A tree is a hierarchical data structure consisting of nodes connected by edges, with one root node at the top. Trees are used in databases, file systems, and more.

levels.title: Graph
levels.description: A graph is a data structure made up of nodes (vertices) and connections (edges). Graphs are used in social networks, maps, and recommendation systems.

levels.title: Binary Search
levels.description: Binary search is an efficient algorithm for finding a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search range in half. Time complexity is O(log n).

levels.title: Sorting Algorithms
levels.description: Sorting algorithms arrange data in a specific order, such as ascending or descending. Examples include Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, and Quick Sort.

levels.title: Hash Table
levels.description: A hash table is a data structure that maps keys to values for fast lookups using hash functions. It is the foundation of many programming languages' objects and dictionaries.

levels.title: Dynamic Programming
levels.description: Dynamic programming is a technique for solving problems by breaking them down into simpler overlapping subproblems and storing solutions to avoid repeated calculations.

levels.title: Greedy Algorithm
levels.description: A greedy algorithm builds up a solution piece by piece, always choosing the option that offers the most immediate benefit.

levels.title: Design Patterns
levels.description: Design patterns are common solutions to recurring software design problems. Examples include Singleton, Observer, and Factory patterns.

levels.title: Observer Pattern
levels.description: The Observer pattern allows objects to subscribe to changes in another object, enabling reactive programming.

levels.title: Microservices
levels.description: Microservices architecture splits a large application into smaller, independent services that communicate over APIs, making systems scalable and easier to maintain.
levels.example:
GET /users-service/api/users
GET /orders-service/api/orders

levels.title: Load Balancing
levels.description: Load balancing distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers to ensure reliability and performance.

levels.title: Caching
levels.description: Caching stores frequently accessed data in memory to improve performance and reduce database load.

levels.title: Distributed Systems
levels.description: A distributed system is a network of independent computers that work together as a single system, often used for scalability and fault tolerance.
levels.example: Examples: Google Search, Netflix Streaming, AWS Cloud

levels.title: Event-Driven Architecture
levels.description: In event-driven architecture, services communicate by producing and consuming events, allowing for loose coupling and asynchronous communication.

levels.title: CI/CD
levels.description: Continuous Integration (CI) and Continuous Deployment (CD) are practices for automatically testing and deploying code to production environments.

levels.title: Machine Learning Basics
levels.description: Machine learning enables software to learn from data and make predictions without explicit programming. Common algorithms include linear regression and decision trees.

levels.title: Cloud Computing
levels.description: Cloud computing provides access to computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, and networking over the internet. It enables on-demand scalability and pay-as-you-go pricing.

Examples of Cloud Providers:

levels.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS

IaaS: AWS EC2
PaaS: Google App Engine

levels.title: Serverless Computing
levels.description: Serverless computing allows developers to run code without managing servers. Cloud providers automatically allocate resources and scale as needed.

levels.title: Virtualization
levels.description: Virtualization allows multiple virtual machines (VMs) to run on a single physical server, optimizing resource usage and improving flexibility.

levels.title: Message Queue

levels.title: CDN (Content Delivery Network)
levels.description: A CDN stores cached copies of content on servers distributed worldwide, improving website performance and reducing latency.

levels.title: WebSocket

levels.title: JWT (JSON Web Token)
levels.description: JWT is a compact token format used to securely transmit information between parties, often used for authentication and authorization.

levels.title: Encryption
levels.description: Encryption converts data into an unreadable format to protect it from unauthorized access. Common algorithms include AES and RSA.

levels.title: SSL/TLS
levels.description: SSL/TLS protocols secure communication over the internet using encryption, ensuring privacy and data integrity.

levels.title: Firewall

levels.title: Zero Trust Security

levels.title: Blockchain

levels.title: Distributed Ledger

levels.title: Load Testing
levels.description: Load testing measures how an application performs under high traffic, helping identify bottlenecks and optimize performance.
levels.example: Tools: Apache JMeter, Locust, k6

levels.title: Rate Limiting
levels.description: Rate limiting controls the number of requests a user can make to an API within a given time to prevent abuse and ensure stability.
levels.example:
Example:
Limit each user to 100 requests per minute.

levels.title: Edge Computing
levels.description: Edge computing brings computation and data storage closer to the user or device, reducing latency and improving speed.
levels.example: Use cases: IoT devices, autonomous vehicles.

levels.title: Machine Learning Operations (MLOps)
levels.description: MLOps is the practice of deploying, monitoring, and maintaining machine learning models in production environments.
levels.example:
Pipeline:
1. Model Training
2. Model Deployment
3. Monitoring Performance

levels.title: Artificial Intelligence
levels.description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the simulation of human intelligence by machines, allowing them to learn, reason, and make decisions.
levels.example:
Applications:
- Chatbots
- Self-driving cars
- Recommendation systems

levels.title: Neural Networks
levels.description: Neural networks are algorithms inspired by the human brain, used in deep learning to recognize patterns and process complex data.
levels.example: Example frameworks: TensorFlow, PyTorch

levels.title: Deep Learning
levels.description: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning using multi-layer neural networks for tasks like image recognition and natural language processing.
levels.example: Use case: Detecting objects in images.

levels.title: Big Data
levels.description: Big data involves processing and analyzing massive datasets that are too large for traditional tools to handle efficiently.
levels.example: Technologies: Hadoop, Apache Spark, Google BigQuery

levels.title: Data Lake
levels.description: A data lake is a centralized repository for storing large volumes of raw data in various formats for future processing and analysis.
levels.example: AWS S3 is commonly used as a data lake storage solution.

levels.title: Data Warehouse
levels.description: A data warehouse stores structured, processed data optimized for business intelligence and analytics.
levels.example: Examples: Amazon Redshift, Snowflake, Google BigQuery

levels.title: DevSecOps
levels.description: DevSecOps integrates security practices into DevOps workflows to ensure security is addressed throughout the development lifecycle.
levels.example: Security checks are run automatically during CI/CD pipeline.

levels.title: Web Assembly (WASM)
levels.description: WebAssembly is a binary instruction format that enables running high-performance applications in web browsers.
levels.example: Use case: Running C++ code in a browser.

levels.title: Quantum Computing
levels.description: Quantum computing uses principles of quantum mechanics to perform complex computations much faster than classical computers.
levels.example: Quantum algorithms like Shor's algorithm can factor large numbers exponentially faster.

levels.title: Federated Learning
levels.description: Federated learning is a machine learning approach where data remains on local devices, and only model updates are shared, enhancing privacy.
levels.example: Used by Google Keyboard to improve predictions without sending user data.

levels.title: Web 3.0
levels.description: Web 3.0 is the decentralized web that aims to give users more control over their data using blockchain and peer-to-peer networks.
levels.example: Examples: Decentralized apps (dApps), IPFS

levels.title: Introduction to DSA
levels.description: Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) form the foundation of efficient problem-solving in programming. Understanding DSA helps you write optimized code, improve performance, and tackle real-world challenges like search engines, social media feeds, and AI systems.

levels.title: Big-O Notation
levels.description: Big-O notation describes the performance and efficiency of an algorithm. It measures how runtime or space requirements grow as the input size increases. Common complexities include O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), and O(n^2).

levels.title: Arrays
levels.description: Arrays store multiple values in a single variable. They allow fast access to elements by index and are fundamental for building other data structures. Operations include insertion, deletion, traversal, and searching.

levels.title: Linked List
levels.description: A linked list is a linear data structure where elements (nodes) are connected using pointers. It is useful for dynamic memory allocation and efficient insertion/deletion compared to arrays.

levels.title: Stacks
levels.description: A stack follows the LIFO (Last In, First Out) principle. Elements are added and removed from the top only. Commonly used in undo operations, recursion, and expression evaluation.

levels.title: Queues
levels.description: A queue follows the FIFO (First In, First Out) principle. Elements are added to the rear and removed from the front. Useful in task scheduling, print queues, and order processing.

levels.title: Hash Tables
levels.description: Hash tables store key-value pairs for fast lookups and insertions. They use a hashing function to map keys to specific locations in memory, making operations efficient on average.

levels.title: Recursion
levels.description: Recursion is a process where a function calls itself to solve a smaller instance of the problem. It's widely used in tree traversal, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and backtracking.

levels.title: Trees
levels.description: Trees are hierarchical data structures with nodes connected by edges. Common types include binary trees, binary search trees, and AVL trees. They're used in databases, file systems, and AI.

levels.title: Graphs
levels.description: Graphs consist of nodes (vertices) connected by edges. They can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. Used in social networks, navigation systems, and network routing.

levels.title: Sorting Algorithms
levels.description: Sorting arranges data in a specific order. Common algorithms include Bubble Sort, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, and Insertion Sort. They vary in complexity and use cases.

levels.title: Searching Algorithms
levels.description: Searching algorithms help find elements in a dataset. Common types include Linear Search and Binary Search, each with different performance characteristics.

levels.title: Dynamic Programming
levels.description: Dynamic Programming (DP) is an optimization technique for solving problems by breaking them down into overlapping subproblems and storing solutions to avoid redundant calculations.

levels.title: Greedy Algorithms
levels.description: Greedy algorithms make the best local choice at each step to achieve a global solution. They're used in problems like activity selection, Huffman coding, and minimum spanning trees.

levels.title: Backtracking
levels.description: Backtracking systematically searches for solutions by exploring possibilities and undoing steps when a dead-end is reached. Commonly used in puzzles, mazes, and constraint satisfaction problems.
